title: What the windpipe does
stem: Which of the following correctly describes the function of the windpipe?

options.text: It is a tube that carries air from the nose and mouth to the lungs.
options.pick: Follow the air itself and ask what the tube does to it, not to anything else.
options.why: The windpipe is purely a passageway for air to the lungs.

options.text: It exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide between air and blood.
options.pick: Air passes through it on its way in, so it seems to be where the air meets the body.
options.why: That is the job of the lungs. The windpipe only lets air through.

options.text: It filters, warms and moistens the air before it reaches the lungs.
options.pick: The windpipe is mixed up with the nose, which is the first part the air meets.
options.why: That describes the nose. The windpipe is a passageway and does not change the air.

options.text: It pumps blood containing oxygen to all parts of the body.
options.pick: The windpipe is linked with oxygen, and oxygen is linked with pumping.
options.why: That is the heart. The windpipe carries air, not blood.

title: Air in and air out
stem: Compared to inhaled air, exhaled air contains —

options.text: Less oxygen, more carbon dioxide and more water vapour.
options.pick: The body uses some oxygen and adds carbon dioxide and water vapour.
options.why: Exhaled air still contains oxygen.

options.text: More oxygen and less carbon dioxide.
options.pick: It looks as if the body adds oxygen, the "good" gas, before breathing out.
options.why: The body takes oxygen from the air. Exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide.

options.text: More oxygen and more carbon dioxide.
options.pick: Everything in the air seems to increase because the air has been inside the body.
options.why: The cells use oxygen, so there is less of it in exhaled air.

options.text: Less oxygen and less carbon dioxide.
options.pick: The body seems to take something from both gases.
options.why: The body makes carbon dioxide, so exhaled air has more of it, not less.

title: Where oxygen enters the blood
stem: In which part of the body does oxygen pass from the air into the blood?

options.text: Nose
options.pick: The nose is where air first enters, so it seems to be where oxygen is taken in.
options.why: The nose filters, warms and moistens air. Oxygen passes into the blood in the lungs.

options.text: Lungs
options.pick: Find the organ where air and blood come closest together.
options.why: The lungs are where oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out.

options.text: Windpipe
options.pick: Air travels through it, so it seems to be where oxygen is taken in.
options.why: The windpipe is only a tube. The gas exchange happens in the lungs.

options.text: Heart
options.pick: Oxygen is carried round the body, and the heart is at the middle of it.
options.why: The heart pumps blood. It does not take in oxygen from the air.

title: The path of the air
stem: Which shows the path of air as we breathe in?

options.text: lungs → windpipe → nose
options.pick: The order is read backwards. Usually a guess.
options.why: That is the path of air as we breathe out.

options.text: nose → windpipe → lungs
options.pick: Trace the route from where air enters to where it ends up.
options.why: Air enters through the nose, travels down the windpipe and reaches the lungs.

options.text: nose → lungs → windpipe
options.pick: The windpipe is thought of as a tube after the lungs. Usually a guess.
options.why: The windpipe lies between the nose and the lungs.

options.text: windpipe → nose → lungs
options.pick: The order is mixed up. Usually a guess.
options.why: Air meets the nose first.

title: What the heart does
stem: What is the main function of the heart?

options.text: It takes in oxygen from the air.
options.pick: The heart is linked with oxygen because blood carries it.
options.why: The lungs take in oxygen. The heart pumps the blood.

options.text: It filters, warms and moistens the air.
options.pick: The jobs of the parts are mixed up.
options.why: That is the nose.

options.text: It pumps blood around the body.
options.pick: Ask what would stop happening if the heart stopped.
options.why: The heart pumps blood through the blood vessels to all parts of the body.

options.text: It carries blood to the cells through its own tubes, with no pumping.
options.pick: The heart is mixed up with the blood vessels.
options.why: Blood vessels carry blood. The heart is the pump that pushes the blood along.

title: What blood carries
stem: Which of the following does blood carry around the body?

options.text: Oxygen only
options.pick: Oxygen is the gas everyone talks about, so it seems to be the only thing carried.
options.why: Blood also carries carbon dioxide and digested food.

options.text: Air
options.pick: Breathing in brings air into the body, so air seems to travel in the blood.
options.why: Air stays in the nose, windpipe and lungs. Only some of its gases pass into the blood.

options.text: Carbon dioxide only
options.pick: Blood going back to the lungs is remembered, and blood going out is forgotten.
options.why: Blood also carries oxygen to the cells.

options.text: Oxygen, carbon dioxide and digested food
options.pick: Blood meets the digestive system and the lungs, so expect it to carry what both of them handle.
options.why: Blood vessels transport digested food, oxygen and carbon dioxide around the body.

title: What blood vessels do
stem: Which statement about blood vessels is correct?

options.text: They carry air to the lungs.
options.pick: Both are tubes in the chest, so they seem to do the same job.
options.why: Air is carried by the windpipe. Blood vessels carry blood.

options.text: They pump blood to the body.
options.pick: Pumping and carrying blood are mixed up. Usually a guess.
options.why: The heart pumps. The vessels carry what the heart pushes.

options.text: They carry blood around the body.
options.pick: Think of blood vessels as tubes and ask what travels inside them.
options.why: Blood vessels are the tubes through which blood travels.

options.text: They pass oxygen from the air into the blood.
options.pick: Blood vessels touch the lungs, so they seem to do the exchange themselves.
options.why: The gas exchange happens in the lungs. The vessels carry the blood to and from them.

title: Mist on a cold mirror
stem: Ben breathes out onto a cold mirror and the mirror becomes misty. What does this show about the air he breathed out?

options.text: It contains water vapour.
options.pick: Mist on glass is tiny drops of water, so work back to what must have been in the breath.
options.why: Water vapour in the breath turns into tiny drops of water on the cold mirror.

options.text: It contains no oxygen.
options.pick: Exhaled air is linked with waste, so it seems to be empty of oxygen.
options.why: The mist does not show anything about oxygen. Exhaled air still has oxygen in it.

options.text: It contains only carbon dioxide.
options.pick: Breathing out is linked with carbon dioxide alone.
options.why: Exhaled air is still mostly the same mixture as inhaled air. The mist is not carbon dioxide.

options.text: It is warmer than the mirror, so it cannot contain any gases.
options.pick: Warm air seems different from ordinary air. Usually a guess.
options.why: Exhaled air is a mixture of gases. The mist shows that it has water vapour.

title: Blood leaving the lungs
stem: Blood travels from the heart to the lungs and then back to the heart. Compared with the blood going to the lungs, the blood leaving the lungs has —

options.text: less oxygen and more carbon dioxide.
options.pick: The lungs are thought to use oxygen up, as cells do.
options.why: The cells use the oxygen. In the lungs the blood gains oxygen and loses carbon dioxide.

options.text: more oxygen and less carbon dioxide.
options.pick: Decide what the blood gains and what it loses while it is in the lungs.
options.why: In the lungs oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out of it.

options.text: the same amount of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
options.pick: Blood is thought of as just a carrier that changes nothing.
options.why: Gas exchange in the lungs changes the blood.

options.text: more oxygen and more carbon dioxide.
options.pick: Both seem to increase because the blood has been in the lungs. Usually a guess.
options.why: Carbon dioxide passes out of the blood in the lungs, so there is less of it.

title: What the body cells do with oxygen
stem: What happens to the oxygen that blood brings to the body cells?

options.text: The cells store it for later and make nothing from it.
options.pick: Cells are pictured as stores. Usually a guess.
options.why: The cells use it to release energy.

options.text: The cells breathe it out as oxygen again.
options.pick: Air in and air out are thought to be the same.
options.why: Cells use the oxygen up, so what they give back is carbon dioxide.

options.text: It is used up in the lungs, so the cells do not receive any.
options.pick: The lungs seem to be the only place that uses oxygen.
options.why: The lungs pass oxygen to the blood. The cells are what use it.

options.text: The cells use it to release energy, and they produce carbon dioxide.
options.pick: This is respiration.
options.why: Blood then carries the carbon dioxide back to the lungs.

title: Which system is the heart in?
stem: A pupil says, "The heart is part of the respiratory system because it helps carry oxygen." Which statement is correct?

options.text: The pupil is correct, because the heart moves oxygen to the body.
options.pick: Moving oxygen seems like a respiratory job.
options.why: The heart pumps blood. It does not take part in gas exchange.

options.text: The pupil is not correct, because the heart carries only carbon dioxide.
options.pick: The blood going back to the lungs is remembered.
options.why: Blood from the heart carries oxygen to the cells too.

options.text: The pupil is not correct. The heart is part of the circulatory system and pumps blood, which carries the oxygen.
options.pick: Check which system the heart belongs to, then check where gas exchange actually happens.
options.why: Gas exchange is in the lungs, which belong to the respiratory system.

options.text: The pupil is correct, because the heart is next to the lungs.
options.pick: Being next to each other seems to mean being in the same system.
options.why: Where an organ is does not tell you which system it belongs to.

title: How a fish takes in oxygen
stem: Which part of a fish takes in oxygen from the water?

options.text: Gills
options.pick: Name the part a fish uses in water that does the same job as our lungs do in air.
options.why: Gills take oxygen from the water and give out carbon dioxide into it.

options.text: Lungs
options.pick: Animals that breathe are pictured with lungs.
options.why: Fish take in the oxygen dissolved in water through their gills.

options.text: Fins
options.pick: Fins are the parts seen moving in the water. Usually a guess.
options.why: Fins are for swimming, not for taking in oxygen.

options.text: Nose
options.pick: Breathing is linked with the nose.
options.why: A fish does not breathe air through a nose. Its gills take in oxygen from the water.

title: Plants and humans compared
stem: Which statement about plants and humans is correct?

options.text: Only humans take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.
options.pick: Plants are not seen breathing, so they seem not to use oxygen.
options.why: Plants take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide too, though they do not use lungs.

options.text: Plants take in only carbon dioxide and give out only oxygen.
options.pick: Plants are known for making oxygen.
options.why: Plants also need oxygen to live. In Primary 6 you learn what leaves do with carbon dioxide.

options.text: Plants take in oxygen through lungs, as humans do.
options.pick: Whatever takes in oxygen is pictured with lungs.
options.why: Plants have no lungs. Only some animals, including humans, have them.

options.text: Both plants and humans take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.
options.pick: Both take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide.
options.why: Humans use their lungs, and plants do it through their leaves and other parts.

title: Transport in a human and a plant
stem: How are substances carried around the body of a human and of a plant?

text: blood vessels carry digested food, oxygen and carbon dioxide
options.pick: Humans have blood vessels.
options.why: Plants have tubes that carry food and water.

text: the windpipe carries digested food and oxygen
options.pick: The windpipe is the tube that carries something we need.
options.why: The windpipe carries air only. Blood vessels carry the other substances.

text: blood vessels carry digested food, oxygen and carbon dioxide
plants have no tubes, so each part makes what it needs
options.pick: Plants are not seen to have anything like blood.
options.why: Plants have tubes that carry food and water to the parts that need them.

text: the heart carries digested food and oxygen by itself
options.pick: The heart is thought of as the thing that moves the blood and everything in it.
options.why: The heart only pumps. The blood vessels carry blood and what is in it.
